chapters.title: Getting Ready
chapters.summary: Medical clearances, imaging, and telling the people who need to know.
topics: Medical clearances and specialist coordination: sign-off from cardiology, sleep medicine, and anesthesia given the Klinefelter/testosterone therapy history
3D imaging and surgical simulation: CT scan and a computer-modeled surgical plan showing the exact bone movement Dr. Denis will make
Understanding facial changes: reviewing the predicted before/after simulation so the new profile isn't a surprise later
Work coverage planning: filing FMLA paperwork and handing off active projects to the team at ClassDojo before going dark
Home preparation: wedge pillow, blender, soft-food stock, and confirming who's around for the first week
chapters.psychologyNote: Anticipation and logistics dominate. Name the fear instead of managing around it.
chapters.skillRef: SKILL.md pre-op block — training guidance for this phase

chapters.title: Final Weeks
chapters.summary: Banking the last hard fitness, and turning a house into a recovery ward.
topics: Pre-op appointments: anesthesia consult, final surgical planning review with Dr. Denis, labs/blood work, EKG if required
Pharmacy prep: fill pain meds, antibiotics, and anti-nausea prescriptions ahead of time; get a syringe/feeding kit and saline nasal spray
Mental preparation: read up on week-1 expectations, line up a support person for the first 72 hours, confirm exact leave dates with work
Last hard training block: final long run and final heavy lift session, then start tapering ~10 days out
Logistics: confirm childcare coverage, any travel/rental logistics, file FMLA paperwork with HR
Stocking soft foods: protein shakes, bone broth, Greek yogurt, applesauce, a blender, a wide-mouth water bottle with a straw
chapters.psychologyNote: The last normal weeks. Use them — don't just survive them.

chapters.title: The Week Of
chapters.summary: Final checklist, one last run, and the quiet before it.
topics: Final prep checklist: confirm arrival time with the hospital, arrange a ride there and back, stop any blood thinners/supplements per surgeon instructions, note the last-meal cutoff time, shower with antibacterial soap the night before
What to pack for hospital: insurance card/ID, phone + charger, chapstick, own pillow, current medication list, a button-front shirt (nothing over the head)
Day-before protocols: nothing to eat or drink after midnight (per surgeon), final medication check, recovery station set up at home before leaving

Setting up recovery space at home: recliner or wedge pillow for 30–45° sleep, pre-frozen ice packs, syringe-feeding kit staged, humidifier, blackout curtains, notepad for writing (talking will be hard)
Last run — whatever feels good, no pressure, just closure
chapters.psychologyNote: Adrenaline and dread trade places by the hour. Both are normal.

chapters.title: Surgery Day
chapters.summary: LeFort I + BSSO. In the OR, the recovery room, and the first night.
topics: What happens in the OR: the LeFort I cuts and repositions the upper jaw, the BSSO does the same to the lower jaw, both plated into the new bite
Immediate post-op: waking up swollen and groggy in recovery, moved to a room, first night monitored closely
What family experiences: hours in a waiting room, then seeing a face that doesn't look like the one that went in
Hospital stay: 1–2 nights for pain control, swelling monitoring, and confirming safe breathing before discharge

chapters.title: Hell Week
chapters.summary: Peak swelling, liquid food through a syringe, and not recognizing your own face.
topics: Swelling peak: face at its most swollen around days 2–3, before it starts (slowly) going down
Pain management: prescribed meds on a fixed schedule, not waiting until it hurts to take them
Liquid diet via syringe: jaw wired/banded, all nutrition through a large oral syringe past the back teeth
Sleep at 30–45° angle: propped up on a wedge or recliner to keep swelling down and breathing easier
Breathing difficulties: nasal passages swollen shut, mouth-breathing restricted by the jaw — genuinely hard to get air for a few days
Numbness begins: lips, chin, and cheeks go numb as nerves react to the surgery — expected, not permanent
Can't recognize yourself: the mirror shows someone else's swollen, bruised face for the first several days
chapters.psychologyNote: Regret is universal. Don't judge the surgery yet.

chapters.title: The Fog
chapters.summary: Off the heavy meds, onto soft foods, still nowhere near work-ready.
topics: Swelling slowly improving: still puffy, but visibly less than hell week
Transitioning off heavy pain meds: moving from prescription painkillers to over-the-counter as pain becomes manageable
Soft foods beginning: yogurt, mashed potatoes, blended soups — anything that doesn't need chewing
Still can't work fully: fatigue and meds make more than an hour or two at a screen rough
Fatigue dominates: the body is spending most of its energy on healing, not much left for anything else
Walking 15–20 minutes: flat, easy walks — the only sanctioned activity right now
Numbness persists: still no full feeling in lips/chin, though it may be starting to tingle at the edges
Bruising fades: the classic bruise color cycle, purple to yellow to gone, over these two weeks

chapters.title: Emerging
chapters.summary: The face becomes recognizable again. Week 6 imaging is the first real gate.
topics: Post-op imaging at week 6: X-ray/CT confirms the bones are healing in the right position — the first real green light
Face becoming recognizable: swelling down enough that it looks like your own face again, just different
Soft foods expanding: scrambled eggs, pasta, ground meat — more texture as chewing becomes possible
Can work 4–6 hours: enough energy back for a partial workday at a screen
Walking 30–45 minutes: longer, still-easy walks as stamina returns
Maybe stationary bike: low-impact cardio if the surgeon clears it at the week-6 check
Swelling 50% down: roughly halfway back to normal by feel and by photos
Still zero running: no running yet regardless of how good the legs feel — bone healing sets the pace, not fitness

chapters.title: First Movement
chapters.summary: Surgeon clearance to move again — bike, elliptical, longer walks.
topics: Surgeon clearance checkpoints: each activity upgrade needs an explicit go-ahead, not a guess
Light cross-training: easy bike or elliptical sessions, low-impact, low-intensity
Walking volume increasing: longer and more frequent walks as energy comes back
Face 70% normal: most of the swelling gone, close to a normal look
Energy returning: noticeably more stamina for work and daily life than the fog weeks
Work near-normal: close to a full workday, though still tiring out faster than before
Numbness: watching for the first tingling as nerves regenerate, or noting if it’s still fully numb
chapters.psychologyNote: Impatience peaks. Focus on what you CAN do.

chapters.title: The First Run
chapters.summary: Walk/jog intervals, three months off, and the emotional weight of running again.
topics: Target: mid-December 2026 — the earliest a first jog is realistically on the table
Walk/jog intervals → continuous running: short jog segments inside longer walks, building toward running the whole thing
What it feels like after 3 months off: legs and lungs both rusty — nothing about it will feel like it used to
Monitoring jaw: watching for clenching under effort or jarring from foot strike — either is a stop signal
Emotional weight of running again: the first jog after three months off is bigger than the pace or distance suggests
10–15 miles/week max: a hard ceiling regardless of how good it feels — the 10% rule starts here
chapters.skillRef: SKILL.md Phase 3 weeks 9–12 — exact walk/jog protocol

chapters.title: Building the Base
chapters.summary: January – March 2027. Progressive mileage, the 10% rule, strength coming back.
topics: January – March 2027: three months of steady, unglamorous base-building
Progressive mileage: climbing from roughly 20 to 40 miles per week over the quarter
10% rule: never more than a 10% increase in weekly mileage — no exceptions for feeling good
No intensity yet: all easy pace, no tempo or speed work — pure aerobic volume
Reintroducing strength training: back to the gym for real lifts, starting light and building load
Learning to run with a changed face: adjusting to permanent-feeling numbness and a slightly different jaw while running
Sleep study at 6 months: overnight test to confirm the surgery actually fixed the sleep apnea it was for
chapters.skillRef: SKILL.md Phase 4 (Volume build) — weekly structure, vert reintroduction, strength restart

chapters.title: Return to Self
chapters.summary: April – June 2027. Quality workouts return. Vert returns. Feeling like myself again.
topics: April – June 2027: the quarter where training starts feeling like training again
40–50 mpw: mileage back in the range it was before surgery
Adding back quality workouts: structured sessions return, not just easy miles
Tempo runs, hill work: sustained-effort runs and vert reintroduced carefully
Vert returning: climbing and descending back in the mix after months of flat routes
Strength training full capacity: back to pre-surgery loads on the big lifts
"Feeling like myself again"
chapters.skillRef: SKILL.md Phase 5 (Return to performance); transition to ultra-plan-generator if a race goal exists

chapters.title: Peak Again
chapters.summary: Full training capacity, first race back, and the one-year assessment.
topics: July – October 2027: the final quarter of the first year, training at full tilt
Full training capacity: no more restrictions — training decisions are fitness decisions again, not recovery decisions
50+ mpw with quality: back to pre-surgery volume, now with real workouts mixed in
First race back: the first competitive or event effort since surgery
One year post-op assessment: final check-in with Dr. Denis on bone healing and bite alignment
Final facial settling: the face finishes its last, subtle changes roughly a year out
Numbness: the one-year mark for knowing whether any lingering numbness is permanent
Reflection: what changed? What did I learn?

chapters.title: First Marathon Back
chapters.summary: A full training cycle, race day, and the complete picture.
topics: Full training cycle: a real periodized build toward a specific race, not just base mileage
Race day: the actual start line, however far out it ends up being
Crossing the finish line: the moment the whole year of rebuilding was pointed at
The complete picture: what a full year of recovery actually adds up to
chapters.skillRef: ultra-plan-generator skill — build the race-specific plan

chapters.title: What I Did Instead of Running
chapters.summary: Twelve weeks without running is twelve weeks of bandwidth for something else.
topics: Main project: learning Frantz Casseus' "Lullaby" on classical guitar
Week-by-week progress documentation: short notes on what got better (or didn’t) each week
From first notes to full piece
Audio clips: short recordings at the start and end to actually hear the progress
Mobility/flexibility deep dive: time to finally work on the stuff running never left room for
Meditation/breathwork practice
Reading list (~20 books)
Writing about 20+ years of design leadership
Piano practice (Casiotone)
Advisory/fractional CDO research: exploring what a fractional creative-leadership role could look like next
chapters.psychologyNote: What have you been saying you don't have time for?
